prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It’s my belief that every man Should do his share of work, And in our economic plan No citizen should shirk. That in return each one should get His meed of fold and food, And feel that all his toil and sweat Is for the common good. It’s my belief that every chap Should have an equal start, And there should be no handicap To hinder his depart; That there be fairness in the fight, And justice in the race, And every lad should have the right To win his proper place. It’s my belief that people should Be neither rich nor poor; That none should suffer servitude, And all should be secure. That wealth is loot, and rank is rot, And foul is class and clan; That to succeed a man may not Exploit his brother man. It’s my belief that heritage And usury are wrong; That each should win a worthy wage And sing an honest song .... Not one like this — for though I rue The wrong of life, I flout it. Alas! I’m not prepared to do A goddam thing about it.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- Every person should contribute their fair share of work and receive enough food, resources, and dignity in return.
- Everyone should have an equal start in life, with fairness, justice, and no artificial barriers to success.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Should, And, That

outputs.L1:
It is my belief that every man  
Should bear his share of work,  
And that, within our economic plan,  
No citizen should shirk.  

That, in return, each one should gain  
His meed of fold and food,  
And feel that all his toil and sweat  
Serve but the common good.  

It is my belief that every chap  
Should have an equal start,  
And that no handicap should stand  
To hinder his depart;  

That fairness should define the fight,  
And justice guide the race,  
And every lad should have the right  
To win his proper place.  

It is my belief that people should  
Be neither rich nor poor;  
That none should suffer servitude,  
And all should be secure.  

That wealth is loot, and rank is rot,  
And foul are class and clan;  
That, to succeed, no man should dare  
Exploit his brother man.  

It is my belief that heritage  
And usury are wrong;  
That each should earn a worthy wage  
And sing an honest song...  

Not one like this—for though I rue  
The wrongs of life, and flout it,  
Alas! I am not prepared to do  
A goddam thing about it.
outputs.L2:
I hold the view that every person ought to carry a fair portion of labor,  
And that within our system of economics, no member of society should avoid responsibility.  
In exchange, each individual should receive a rightful share of shelter and food,  
And should know that their effort and hardship serve the welfare of everyone.

I believe that every fellow should be given the same chance at the beginning,  
With no obstacle placed before him to hold him back from setting out.  
The contest should be conducted fairly, the race governed by justice,  
And every young man should have the opportunity to earn the position that truly belongs to him.

I think people ought to live without extremes of wealth or poverty,  
That no one should be forced into bondage, and everyone should enjoy safety and stability.  
I believe riches are plunder, social status is worthless nonsense,  
And divisions of class or clan are corrupt and ugly.  
No person, in order to prosper, should be allowed to take advantage of another.

I believe inherited privilege and lending for profit are unjust,  
And that everyone should earn a decent wage  
And be able to sing a song of honest living...

But not a song like this one—because although I grieve over life’s injustices  
And openly condemn them,  
Sadly, I am not actually ready  
To do a damn thing to change them.
outputs.L3:
Every person should be expected to contribute their fair share of work to society, according to their ability and circumstances. In return, each person should receive enough food, resources, security, and dignity to live a decent life. A just society is one in which labor is respected and people are not left hungry, degraded, or abandoned while others benefit from their efforts.

Such a society should also give everyone an equal start in life. No one should be held back by unfair social conditions, inherited disadvantage, or artificial barriers to success. Fairness and justice require that people have genuine opportunities to develop their abilities, improve their lives, and participate fully in the community. Success should depend on effort, talent, and character rather than on birth, wealth, or social position.

The speaker imagines a world without extreme divisions between rich and poor. Society should avoid conditions in which some people live in luxury while others suffer in poverty or dependence. It should reject servitude, rigid class hierarchies, and systems that allow one group to exploit another. Human beings should not be reduced to tools for the comfort or profit of others.

Inherited privilege is therefore presented as unjust because it gives certain people advantages they have not earned. Similarly, usury is condemned because it allows wealth to grow through the hardship and dependence of others rather than through productive labor. By contrast, honest work and fair wages are valued as the proper foundation of a moral society. People who work should be treated with respect and should receive compensation that reflects their contribution.

However, the speaker also reveals a serious contradiction. Although he condemns social injustice and recognizes the unfairness of exploitation, poverty, and privilege, he admits that he is not willing to take action against these problems. His beliefs remain moral judgments rather than commitments to change. This admission exposes the gap between criticizing injustice in principle and actually working to correct it in practice.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a speaker who openly claims to believe in economic justice and a fairer social order. The speaker supports the idea that every person should have an equal chance to live well, work with dignity, and benefit from the labor they contribute. In this vision, society should not be built on exploitation, inherited privilege, or rigid class divisions. No one should be allowed to enjoy excessive wealth simply because of birth or social position, while others are trapped in poverty despite their effort and ability. The poem therefore expresses sympathy for ideals such as equality, shared responsibility, and the fair distribution of opportunity.

At the same time, the poem is deeply ironic because the speaker’s beliefs do not lead to action. Although the speaker recognizes that society is unjust and understands the moral arguments for change, they ultimately admit an unwillingness to sacrifice personal comfort or take part in meaningful reform. This confession exposes the distance between approving of justice in theory and committing to it in practice. The poem’s key effect is to criticize not only social inequality itself, but also the passive attitude of those who condemn injustice while continuing to benefit from it or refusing to challenge it. In this way, the poem highlights the conflict between moral ideals and personal self-interest, showing how easy it is to support change abstractly while avoiding the responsibility of helping to bring it about.
outputs.L5:
**Should, And, That**

The words **“should,” “and,”** and **“that”** may seem simple, but they play an important role in everyday communication. We use **“should”** when giving advice, making recommendations, or talking about what is expected. For example, we might say, “You should rest if you feel tired.” This word helps express responsibility, suggestion, or possibility.

The word **“and”** connects ideas, people, actions, or objects. It allows us to build longer and clearer sentences. For example, “She studied hard and passed the exam.” Without **“and,”** our speech and writing would feel disconnected and less natural.

The word **“that”** is also very useful because it helps introduce information or explain something more clearly. For example, “I believe that honesty is important.” It can point to a specific thing, connect clauses, or add meaning to a sentence.

Together, **“should,” “and,”** and **“that”** show how even small words can make language more precise and meaningful. They help us give advice, connect thoughts, and explain ideas in a way that others can easily understand.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical poem in the style of Robert W. Service about socialist ideals, ending with the speaker admitting he won’t actually do anything about them.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Ballad of the Armchair Red**

There’s a fire in my belly for justice,  
There’s a torch in my trembling hand,  
And I’d march with the workers at sunrise  
For the birth of a brotherly land.  
I’d thunder at tyrants and bankers,  
I’d shatter the gilded machine—  
If only the weather were kinder,  
And my slippers were not so serene.

Oh, I’ve read of the mills and the miners,  
Of the children with hunger-pinched cheeks;  
I have sighed over pamphlets and posters,  
I have lectured my friends now for weeks.  
“Let the wealth of the world be for all men!  
Let the idle rich tremble!” I cry—  
Then I order a pastry with coffee  
And let the poor waiter rush by.

I’ve a dream of communes and comrades,  
Of bread with no price at the till,  
Of landlords reduced to mere mortals,  
Of wages that cover the bill.  
I’d gladly give up my possessions,  
Each trinket, each bauble, each gem—  
Though perhaps we should start with my neighbor’s,  
For I’m rather attached to *them*.

There are meetings, I know, in the city,  
Where brave souls make banners and plans;  
They print little leaflets by midnight  
And ink up their diligent hands.  
I would join them in noble devotion,  
I’d stand where the brave banners blow—  
But the tram fare is frankly outrageous,  
And the hall is a long way to go.

So here’s to the dawn of the people,  
To equality’s radiant day;  
May the old world be toppled tomorrow,  
May oppression be swept clean away.  
Yes, comrades, I’m firm in my ardor,  
My principles proudly I state—  
But as for doing something about them,  
Well… I’m terribly busy of late.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhyming political monologue where the narrator praises equality, fair wages, and the common good, but undercuts it with a cynical final confession.
counterfactuals.output:
My friends, I stand for equal ground,  
Where every voice may rise unbound,  
Where no one’s hunger, rent, or wage  
Is left to fate or gilded cage.  

I praise the hands that build and mend,  
The nurse, the driver, teacher, friend;  
A fair day’s pay for honest toil,  
A share of harvest from the soil.  

Let wealth not pool in towers of glass,  
While shadows lengthen where we pass;  
Let common good be more than phrase—  
A lamp to guide our public ways.  

For roads and schools and healing care,  
For cleaner water, cleaner air,  
For dignity in every street,  
For bread enough and warmth and heat.  

Yes, lift the low, restrain the strong,  
Repair the old and open wrong;  
Let justice ring from hill to hood—  
All hail the noble common good.  

And yet, when cheers have filled the hall,  
When banners fold and nightbirds call,  
I’ll tell the truth behind my grin:  
I only preached it all to win.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a vintage-style poem arguing that no one should be rich or poor, wealth and class are unjust, and everyone should work for the common good—then give it a humorous twist ending.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Ballad for the Common Purse**

In days of soot and candlelight,  
When clocks rang cold and clear,  
One man supped on silver plates,  
One gnawed a crust in fear.  

The lord rode by in velvet trim,  
The maid wore patched-up thread;  
Yet both were born of mortal dust,  
And both would one day be dead.  

What justice crowns a golden heir  
For merely drawing breath,  
While honest hands that build the world  
Are bartered down to death?  

No child should wake to empty bowls,  
No mansion mock the street;  
No back be bent beneath a crown,  
No heart beneath defeat.  

Let none be rich as winter kings,  
Let none be poor as rain;  
Let bread and books and firelight warm  
Each windowpane the same.  

Let labor serve the common good,  
Not greed’s devouring mill;  
Let every willing hand find work,  
And every hunger still.  

Away with ranks that teach the soul  
To bow or to command;  
For dignity is not a coin  
To pass from hand to hand.  

So raise the barn, and mend the road,  
And share the harvest’s store;  
Let “mine” and “thine” grow faint and old,  
And “ours” be loved the more.  

Thus all shall toil, and all shall feast,  
And none shall hoard the pie—  
Except, perhaps, Aunt Mabel’s cat,  
Who’s sitting on it. Why?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a ballad-like verse from the perspective of someone who believes in economic justice and equal opportunity, but is too lazy or cowardly to act on those beliefs?
counterfactuals.output:
I wear a ribbon on my coat,  
And speak of bread and land,  
Of every child with shoes and books,  
Of wages fair to hand.  

I curse the lord behind his gate,  
The banker’s polished grin,  
Then close my door when rain comes down  
And let the cold folk in—  

No, not inside; I mean in thought,  
In songs I softly keep,  
While others march through mud and night,  
I turn myself to sleep.  

I know the scales are weighted wrong,  
I know the dice are cast,  
But courage is a costly coin,  
And mine is spent too fast.  

So here I sit with noble words,  
A hearth, a cup, a chair,  
And dream a road made wide for all—  
But never meet them there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem with old-fashioned diction and regular rhyme/meter that sounds like a declaration of egalitarian principles, concluding with “I’m not prepared to do a goddam thing about it.”
counterfactuals.output:
Let lord and lackey, prince and thrall,  
Stand equal in the morning’s light;  
No crown shall make a man more tall,  
Nor rags diminish any right.  

The ploughman’s hand, the scholar’s pen,  
The smith beside the merchant’s stall,  
Are fashioned of one clay; and men  
By birth are brethren, one and all.  

Let no man’s hunger gild another,  
Nor any child be bought or sold;  
Each maid a sister, each a brother,  
Each heart as worth its weight in gold.  

So swear I, by the common air,  
By hearth and field, by sea and sky:  
The world is wrong, the wrong is bare—  
I’m not prepared to do a goddam thing about it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
